independentSolutionSummary: Model the six people as a two-colouring of K6. From any vertex, at least three of the five incident edges share a colour. If any edge among those three endpoints has that colour, it closes a monochromatic triangle; otherwise the three internal edges all have the opposite colour. For five people, a 5-cycle and its complement give a colouring with no monochromatic triangle.
computationalChecks: Exhaustive enumeration of all 2^15 two-colourings of K6; explicit 5-cycle counterexample for K5.

independentSolutionSummary: For one new guest, shift old guest n to room n+1 and use room 1. For one countably infinite bus, send old guest n to room 2n and bus guest k to room 2k-1. The two image sets are disjoint and exhaust the positive integers, so the assignment is collision-free and complete. Countably many buses can be handled by any explicit bijection from N×N to N after reserving a countable subset for existing guests.

Encode two colours by 0 and 1. The back prisoner announces the parity of the 99 visible hats. Each later prisoner subtracts the visible hats and the already-deduced hats behind them from that announced parity, uniquely determining their own bit. Induction gives correctness for prisoners 99 through 1; only the first speaker is not guaranteed.
computationalChecks: Exhaustive verification of the parity strategy for every hat assignment in a six-prisoner analogue.

independentSolutionSummary: A standard checkerboard colouring gives 32 squares of each colour. The specified opposite corners have the same colour, so removing them leaves a 30/32 imbalance. Every edge-adjacent domino covers one square of each colour, hence 31 dominoes would require 31 of each colour, which is impossible.

Pair each positive divisor d of n with n/d. This involution has a fixed point exactly when d^2=n. A nonsquare therefore has only two-element divisor pairs, while a square has exactly one fixed divisor sqrt(n), proving the parity characterization in both directions. The prime-exponent product formula gives the same equivalence.

Assume a complete finite prime list p1,...,pk and set N=p1...pk+1. N is greater than 1, so it has a prime divisor q. Every listed prime leaves remainder 1 on N and therefore cannot be q, contradicting completeness. N itself need not be prime.

Inductively 0<=x_n<=2. On that interval, sqrt(2+x)>=x because (2-x)(x+1)>=0, so the sequence is increasing and bounded and therefore converges. Passing to the limit gives L^2-L-2=0, and nonnegativity selects L=2. The stated error identity follows by rationalizing 2-sqrt(2+x).
computationalChecks: Numerical identity and invariant-interval sweep for x in {0,0.1,...,2}; this is a regression check, not the proof.

independentSolutionSummary: The core claim follows because the degree sum is twice the edge count, hence even, so the number of odd summands is even. Equivalently, starting from the empty graph, each added edge flips degree parity at exactly two endpoints.

findings.summary: The `components` extension asks the candidate to discuss Euler trails without defining the object or stating the intended theorem.
findings.evidence: The candidate-visible problem supplies only the graph model. The extension introduces an additional graph-theory concept not supplied by the family; under the Wave 2 prerequisite rule it should define the term and a precise target, or be removed.

independentSolutionSummary: Write each selected integer uniquely as 2^k times an odd number. There are exactly n possible odd parts among 1,...,2n, so n+1 selected numbers force two with the same odd part. Ordering their exponents of 2 shows the smaller divides the larger. Sharpness is witnessed by {n+1,...,2n}.
computationalChecks: Exhaustive enumeration of every (n+1)-subset of {1,...,2n} for n<=6 confirms a divisibility pair in all tested cases.

findings.summary: The `poset-view` extension relies on the definition and language of partially ordered sets without supplying it.
findings.evidence: The core family assumes only elementary divisibility and pigeonhole reasoning. `Interpret the problem as ... a divisibility poset` is not self-contained under the stated prerequisites.

independentSolutionSummary: Let g(x)=f(x)-x. Continuity of f makes g continuous, while f([0,1])⊆[0,1] gives g(0)>=0 and g(1)<=0. Endpoint equality already gives a fixed point; otherwise IVT supplies an interior zero. The same argument works on any interval [a,b].

findings.summary: The higher-dimensional extension invokes Brouwer's fixed-point theorem as expected discussion content without providing the higher-dimensional statement or needed concepts.
findings.evidence: The core problem explicitly grants IVT, but the stretch prompt jumps to an advanced theorem outside the supplied assumptions. It should be reframed as interviewer background only or made self-contained.

independentSolutionSummary: Let S_k=a_1+...+a_k. If some S_k is 0 modulo n, that prefix is a valid block. Otherwise n prefix sums occupy only n-1 nonzero residue classes, so two are congruent; their difference is a nonempty consecutive block divisible by n. Equivalently include S_0=0 and apply pigeonhole to n+1 residues.
computationalChecks: Exhaustive test of all length-n sequences over {-2,-1,0,1,2} for n<=5.

findings.summary: The `cyclic-blocks` extension does not state a determinate mathematical claim.
findings.evidence: `Explore the analogous statement for cyclic consecutive blocks` leaves open whether ordinary blocks are allowed, whether wrap-around is required, and what must be proved. Under the Wave 2 solvability gate the extension needs explicit quantifiers and a target.

independentSolutionSummary: With position vectors, M_A=(B+C)/2 and G=(A+B+C)/3 satisfy G=A+(2/3)(M_A-A), so G lies two-thirds of the way from A to M_A. Cyclic repetition places the same G on all three medians and yields the 2:1 ratio.

findings.summary: The declared `mass-points` approach assumes a nonstandard barycentric/mass-points method that is neither defined nor listed as a prerequisite.
findings.evidence: The vector route is self-contained, but Wave 2 requires every intended approach to be valid under intended knowledge assumptions. The mass-points branch should define its balancing rule or be removed as an authored route.

independentSolutionSummary: Additivity yields f(0)=0, oddness, integer homogeneity, and then rational homogeneity f(q)=qf(1). Monotonicity gives c=f(1)>=0 and lets rational bounds r<x<s squeeze f(x) between cr and cs, proving f(x)=cx for every real x.

findings.summary: The `pathological-note` extension requires the concept of a basis of R over Q (and the associated existence construction) without supplying that machinery.
findings.evidence: The core family is elementary additive/monotone reasoning. Asking why nonlinear additive functions depend on a Hamel basis is not self-contained for the intended prerequisite level.

independentSolutionSummary: For the reflection route, unrestricted paths number C(2n,n). A bad path has a first Up step from y=x to y=x+1; swapping Right/Up on the prefix through that step gives a bijection with paths having n+1 Right and n-1 Up steps, so bad paths number C(2n,n-1) and the desired count is C(2n,n)/(n+1).
computationalChecks: Enumeration of all monotone paths through n=8 matches C(2n,n)/(n+1).

findings.summary: The candidate-visible statement never specifies that n is a nonnegative integer (or positive integer).
findings.evidence: The endpoint (n,n), the number of unit steps, and the binomial formula require an integer parameter. The domain should be explicit rather than inferred.

findings.summary: The declared Catalan-recurrence approach does not independently derive the requested closed-form count.
findings.evidence: Its branch only says to obtain the Catalan recurrence; the shared final milestone then says to count bad paths and subtract, which is reflection-specific. Hints 3-5 are also reflection-only. Either the recurrence route must include a derivation of the closed form or it should not be represented as a complete alternate approach.

findings.summary: The reflection bijection is correct, but the inverse is described only as locating a 'corresponding shifted imbalance'.
findings.evidence: This is not a false claim; for auditability the inverse should identify the first point with x=y+1 in the transformed path and reflect the corresponding prefix.

independentSolutionSummary: Factor f(x)-f(a)=(x-a)(x²+ax+a²-1). Other equal-height inputs are roots of q_a(x)=x²+ax+a²-1 other than a. Its discriminant 4-3a² gives zero, one-double, or two quotient roots, while q_a(a)=3a²-1 isolates the separate stationary duplication at |a|=1/sqrt(3). For x³-cx the corresponding thresholds are |a|=2sqrt(c/3) and |a|=sqrt(c/3).
computationalChecks: Representative substitutions at a=0, ±1/sqrt(3), ±2/sqrt(3), and 2 matched the authored distinct-input classification.

independentSolutionSummary: With y_n=1/(1-x_n), direct algebra gives y_{n+1}=y_n+1, hence x_n=1-1/(n+y_0). For x_0<1, y_0>0, so x_n increases to 1. For x_0>1 the orbit becomes undefined exactly when y_0 is a negative integer, equivalently when an iterate reaches x=2; otherwise the translated orbit remains defined and ultimately approaches 1.
computationalChecks: Representative starts x_0=0, 1/2, 6/5, 3/2, 17/10, and 3 matched the explicit transformed recurrence and the predicted pole cases.

independentSolutionSummary: For |a|<2 the radicand is positive on R. Rationalization gives the right limit a/2, while factoring |x| on the left gives R_a(x)=-2x-a/2+o(1). The derivative is negative: it is immediate when 2x+a<=0, and otherwise squaring the positive comparison reduces to a²<4. Thus the range is (a/2,∞). At a=±2 the radical is an absolute value, and for |a|>2 the radicand domain splits into two exterior intervals.
computationalChecks: A numerical derivative sweep for a=-1.9,-1,0,1,1.9 over x in [-10,10] stayed negative, consistent with the independent analytic sign proof.

independentSolutionSummary: The original equation has the isolated solution (0,0). Every other solution has x,y nonzero and satisfies 1/x²+1/y²=1, so |x|,|y|>1 with asymptotes x=±1,y=±1. On the nonzero branches, x²+y²>=4 with equality at the four points (±sqrt(2),±sqrt(2)); globally, however, the origin itself is the unique closest point to the origin.
computationalChecks: Direct substitution confirms (0,0) satisfies the original equation, while the four (±sqrt(2),±sqrt(2)) points lie on the nonzero branches at squared distance 4.
Re-reviewed Cantor head b9fe1d9cdd3d0216bc3f4a0fa350824a97f36b73 after the inline fixes; the scaled extension now also asks specifically for closest points on the nonzero branches.

findings.evidence: Fixed on Cantor head b9fe1d9cdd3d0216bc3f4a0fa350824a97f36b73: the milestone now explicitly minimizes on the nonzero branches and calls the four sqrt(2) points the closest points of those branches.

findings.summary: The common-error description falsely states that x=0 or y=0 cannot satisfy the original equation.
findings.evidence: Fixed on Cantor head b9fe1d9cdd3d0216bc3f4a0fa350824a97f36b73: the common-error text now says division before checking the axes deletes the isolated solution (0,0).

independentSolutionSummary: Squaring gives a_{n+1}²=a_n²+2+1/a_n², hence a_n²>=a_0²+2n and divergence. Summation yields a_n²=a_0²+2n+sum 1/a_k²; the lower bound makes the error sum at most logarithmic, so a_n²/(2n)->1 and positivity gives a_n/sqrt(2n)->1. The same argument with c>0 gives the stated sqrt(2cn) scaling.

The graph equation is (x+1)(y+1)=a+1. For a≠-1 it is symmetric in x,y and direct composition gives T_a(T_a(x))=x; moreover T_a(x) never equals -1, so the second application is defined. Fixed points satisfy (x+1)²=a+1. At a=-1 the original formula instead collapses to the constant -1 on R\{-1}, so it has no valid fixed point and cannot be iterated twice.

findings.summary: The stretch extension uses the term involution without defining it candidate-visibly.
findings.evidence: The core already establishes the property T(T(x))=x, so the extension is mathematically viable; rephrasing the extension in terms of that property would remove the vocabulary assumption.

independentSolutionSummary: Necessity is sum_v outdeg(v)=|E|, so the prescribed parity sum must equal |E| modulo 2. For sufficiency, orient non-tree edges arbitrarily, root a spanning tree, and process non-root vertices from leaves upward; each parent edge is the last parity switch for its child. Once every non-root parity is correct, the global parity identity forces the root. Componentwise application gives the disconnected extension.

From p|(n²+n+1), n³≡1 mod p. For p≠3, n is neither 0 nor 1 modulo p; period two together with period three would force n≡1. Thus multiplication by n partitions the p-1 nonzero residues into 3-cycles, so p≡1 mod 3. The n²+1 transfer similarly gives 4-cycles for odd p and hence p≡1 mod 4.

Containment gives a rooted inclusion tree. Because every singleton is present, the leaves are exactly the n singletons and maximal proper children of any non-singleton node are disjoint and cover it, so each internal node has at least two children. Edge counting gives I≤L-1 and |F|≤2n-1; equality is exactly the full-binary case. The missing-singletons extension retains the same bound, e.g. by adjoining missing singletons (and U if needed) without breaking laminarity.

Translate a chosen element to 0. Midpoint closure then gives closure under halving; on the finite translated set, halving is injective and hence bijective, so doubling is also closed. Averaging then doubling gives addition, and finiteness supplies inverses. Thus the translate is an additive subgroup. Modulo a prime the only possibilities are {0} and the full group; for odd composite moduli the solutions are exactly cosets of additive subgroups.

A nonempty balanced finite digraph contains a directed cycle; deleting a cycle preserves indegree/outdegree balance, so induction decomposes all edges into directed cycles. Adding t→s balances the stated one-unit source/sink graph. Removing that artificial edge from its decomposition cycle leaves an s→t path. With r artificial return edges, breaking the affected cycles yields r s→t paths plus cycles.

Over F2, final lamps satisfy x_i=y_i+y_{i-1}+y_{i-2}. The zero-effect recurrence y_i=y_{i-1}+y_{i-2} has period three. Cyclic closure gives a trivial kernel when 3∤n and a four-element kernel when 3|n. Hence every target is uniquely reachable in the former case; in the latter, the image has size 2^(n-2), exactly matching the configurations whose three residue-class parities are equal, and every reachable target has four realizing move subsets.
computationalChecks: Exhaustive enumeration of all move subsets for n=3,...,10 confirmed kernel size, image size, residue-class parity obstruction, and realizing-subset multiplicity.

independentSolutionSummary: Equidistance gives ax+by+cz=0; after x=au,y=bv,z=cw this is αu+βv+γw=0 in the cube with α=a²≤β=b²≤γ=c². Direct edge-family tests show four distinct section vertices when γ≥α+β and six when γ<α+β, with equality causing multiple edge incidences to coalesce at cube vertices. For a=b=c the six vertices are the permutations of (1,-1,0), forming a regular hexagon.
computationalChecks: Enumerated all cube-edge intersections for representative γ>α+β, γ=α+β, γ<α+β, and cube cases; distinct vertex counts were 4,4,6,6 respectively.

independentSolutionSummary: A point X=(x,y) is on the diameter circle exactly when r²=ax+by. With b=1-a/2 and a∈[0,2], the right side ranges over the interval between y and 2x, so existence is equivalent to (r²-y)(r²-2x)≤0. This is precisely the closure of the symmetric difference of the two endpoint disks. The λ,L transfer replaces the endpoint values by Ly/λ and Lx.
computationalChecks: Checked a rectangular grid of sample points against the exact solved parameter a and the sign-product criterion; the two membership tests agreed.

independentSolutionSummary: For unit endpoint vectors u,v, OM²=|(u+v)/2|²=(1+u·v)/2. The regular-polygon vertex sum is 0, so conditioned on a fixed endpoint and a distinct second endpoint, the average dot product is -1/(n-1), giving (n-2)/(2(n-1)). Independent draws with replacement have E[U·V]=E[U]·E[V]=0 and therefore mean 1/2.
computationalChecks: Enumerated all unordered vertex pairs for regular n-gons with n=3,...,14; the empirical mean matched (n-2)/(2(n-1)).

independentSolutionSummary: On a line, block starts are position 1 when selected plus each later 0→1 transition, so E[X]=1/2+(n-1)/4=(n+1)/4. On a circle ordinary blocks equal cyclic 0→1 transitions except the all-selected configuration, adding the correction 2^-n; thus E[X]=n/4+2^-n. Replacing 1/2 by p gives p+(n-1)p(1-p) and np(1-p)+p^n.
computationalChecks: Exhaustive enumeration of all subsets for n=2,...,7 matched both the line and circular expectation formulas.

independentSolutionSummary: A finite nonnegative difference-closed set with at least two elements has a least positive d. Repeated subtraction of d from any x in the set leaves a remainder in the set below d, forcing remainder 0; hence every element is a nonnegative integer multiple of d. Repeated subtraction from the maximum fills every multiple up to it. Conversely such finite initial arithmetic grids are difference-closed. Signed difference closure would generate all integer multiples of any nonzero element, contradicting finiteness, so only {0} remains.

After n fair halvings the left/right word is a uniformly distributed n-bit integer K, and M_n=(K+1/2)/2^n. This gives mean 1/2 and variance (1-4^-n)/12. With right-half probability p, digitwise expectation gives E[K]=p(2^n-1) and E[M_n]=p+(1/2-p)2^-n. Endpoint conventions matter only for containment questions, not the midpoint distribution.

Under an arrivals-then-service convention the correct recurrence is q_{n+1}=max(0,q_n+a_n-s), and away from the reflecting boundary the two-minute drift is a+b-2s. Positive drift eventually grows, negative drift forces a visit to the reflecting boundary, and zero drift can sustain a periodic positive orbit. However the exact emptying question is a function of the initial queue and starting phase, which the candidate-visible statement does not specify.

findings.summary: The modelling statement omits the parameter and initial-state assumptions needed to make the exact emptying question well-posed.
findings.evidence: The prompt introduces a,b,s only through story language and never introduces q_0 or fixes the phase at which q_0 is measured. Exact emptiness depends on q_0 and phase. State explicit nonnegative-integer customer/capacity assumptions (with s>0 if intended), q_0≥0, and a starting phase, or narrow the task to a qualitative dependence statement.
